text: Lesson 1 made the case that ServiceNow is a platform, not just ITSM. This lesson gives you the actual shape of that platform — a four-layer mental model you'll keep returning to for the rest of this course and the courses after it. Nothing here needs to be memorized in depth yet; each layer gets its own deep-dive later. For now, the goal is just knowing the layers exist and roughly what belongs in each one.

Layer one is the database layer, built on what ServiceNow calls the Glide Data Model. Every piece of data — every incident, every user, every Configuration Item — lives in a table. Tables can extend other tables, the way incident extends the base task table and inherits its common fields, and tables relate to each other through reference fields. This layer is purely structural: it defines what data exists and how it's shaped, with no behavior of its own.

Layer two is the application layer — the forms people fill out, the lists they scan through, and the logic behind them. Business Rules are server-side logic that run on insert, update, delete, or query, like auto-assigning a new incident based on its category. Client Scripts run in the browser as someone fills out a form. Script Includes are reusable server-side script libraries other logic can call into instead of duplicating code.

Layer three is the UI layer — how all of that gets rendered on screen. ServiceNow has been through more than one UI generation: the long-standing Classic UI, also called UI16, and the newer Next Experience, including Workspaces, a more modern, configurable interface ServiceNow has been pushing customers toward, especially for agent-facing work. Both generations render the exact same tables, forms, and logic underneath — the UI layer is a presentation choice, not a different platform.

The last piece isn't stacked on top of the others — it's a set of services that reach into every layer at once. Access Control Lists, or ACLs, govern who can read, write, create, or delete specific tables, fields, or records, no matter which UI someone is using. Flow Designer builds multi-step automated processes spanning tables, approvals, and notifications. And integration, through REST APIs and IntegrationHub, is how data moves in and out of the instance to and from other systems.

Each of those cuts across the database, application, and UI layers at once, which is why they're treated as platform services rather than a single layer in the stack. Next up: opening the Application Navigator and actually finding your way around a real instance.
